content: Primula veris, commonly known as cowslip (and also referred to by its synonym Primula officinalis Hill), is a flowering plant belonging to the genus Primula. This species is native to much of temperate Europe and Asia. However, it is absent from more northern regions, such as most of north-west Scotland, though it reappears in the northernmost areas of Sutherland and Orkney. The plant is a low-growing, herbaceous perennial that forms a rosette of leaves measuring 5–15 cm in length and 2–6 cm in width. Its deep yellow flowers bloom during the spring, typically between April and May. These flowers are arranged in clusters of 10–30 on a single stem that grows to a height of 5–20 cm. Each individual flower measures 9–15 mm in diameter. Rarely, red-flowered variants of the plant can also be found. Cowslip is often found in more open habitats compared to Primula vulgaris (commonly known as primrose). It thrives in open fields, meadows, coastal dunes, and clifftops. The plant is frequently included in wildflower seed mixes used for landscaping purposes, such as along motorway banks and other civil engineering earthworks, where it often grows in dense stands. Cowslip can sometimes be mistaken for the closely related Primula elatior (commonly known as oxlip). While the two species share a similar general appearance, oxlip is distinguished by its larger, pale yellow flowers that resemble those of the primrose, as well as a corolla tube that lacks folds. Cowslip is a favored food source for wild rabbits. Folklore and Herbalism Cowslip has been used medicinally for its diuretic, expectorant, and antispasmodic properties. It has also been employed in the treatment of headaches, whooping cough, tremors, and other conditions. However, it can cause irritant effects in individuals who are allergic to it. Historically, cowslips were used to make wine and to flavor conventional wines. An ancient name for the plant is paigle, though the origin of this term is unknown. Another name, herb Peter, is derived from a legend about Saint Peter dropping the keys to the Gates of Heaven, with cowslips said to have sprung up from the spot where the keys fell. In the 19th century, cowslips were used to create garlands for maypoles. The cowslip is also recognized as the county flower of four English counties: Essex, Northamptonshire, Surrey, and Worcestershire.
